To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Connectionism does not provide a viable cognitive architecture, but that Connectionist models may be useful in understanding the implementation of a Classical cognitive architecture in the brain.

(1) Connectionism is not a theory of mind/brain architecture; it is a theory of how neural structures are organized, and (2) Connectionism is a theory of mind-brain architecture only on the assumption that neural structures are organized in such a way as to implement a Classical architecture at the cognitive level.
(a) Connectionism is not a viable theory of cognitive architecture, (b) Connectionism is a viable theory of neural architecture.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following question: Is Connectionism a new approach to cognitive science, or is it a new approach to neuroscience? We argue that it is the latter, and that Connectionists are mistaken in thinking that their work has any implications for cognitive architecture.
the question of whether Connectionist models can be reconciled with Classical cognitive science.
the question of whether the mind is a classical or connectionist computer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

(i) Connectionism provides the most plausible account of the neural implementation of cognitive architecture; and (ii) Connectionism does not provide an adequate account of the cognitive architecture itself.
the Connectionist approach is not a theory of cognitive architecture at all.
Connectionism is a promising theory of neural implementation but not of cognitive architecture.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Connectionism provides a powerful and promising account of the neurophysiology of cognition, but not of the cognitive architecture that underlies cognitive processes.
Connectionist models may be useful in the study of the brain, but not for the study of mind.
, if we are right, Connectionism is not an alternative to Classical cognitive science; it is a theory about how Classical cognitive architectures are implemented.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the debate between Connectionism and Classicalism is a debate about the architecture of the cognitive mind/brain, not about its implementation in the brain.
, while Connectionism is not a viable model of cognitive architecture, it may provide a model of neural architecture.

, if Connectionism is not to be a'mere' computational metaphor, then it must be understood as providing a theory of the neural implementation of cognitive architecture, and not as providing a theory at the cognitive level of representation.
